source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Founding paper. Dynamic benchmark: 1,000 questions from 9 sources, only about unresolved future events, so no leakage. Humans forecast a random 200-question subset.
numbers: 1,000 LLM questions; 200 human subset. 39 superforecasters, 500 public (Prolific/Facebook, ~49 answers per question). 7 baselines: zero-shot, scratchpad, scratchpad+news, each with and without crowd freeze values.
limits: Median of each human group is scored. Human groups surveyed once (July 2024). Freeze values only help market questions.
agent_relevance: Test our agent on unresolved questions, never on resolved ones, and log forecasts for later scoring (S9).

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Headline gap. Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM on the 200-question set.
numbers: Overall Brier: superforecasters 0.096; public 0.121 (p<0.001 vs supers); best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (p<0.001 vs supers). Best LLM without crowd forecasts 0.136.
limits: Top LLMs had the human crowd price for market questions, so 0.122 is helped by humans. Overall score = mean of dataset Brier and market Brier.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM result depended on a human-crowd input. Our agent should add an outside anchor when one exists.

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Combination (conjunction) questions widen the gap.
numbers: With combos: supers 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. Gap supers vs GPT-4o 0.054, twice the 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4.
limits: Combo questions are built by the benchmark from base events; their dependence is modeled only approximately.
agent_relevance: Joint-probability reasoning is a weak point. Add a coherence check across linked claims (G5, code does the arithmetic).

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Prompt and information effects on the 1,000-question set: scratchpad prompts and crowd values helped; fresh news did not.
numbers: Most top models use scratchpad prompt plus crowd freeze values. Text: Access to recent topical news ... did not improve performance. GPT-4o news+freeze (scratchpad) 0.143 overall in appendix; GPT-4o freeze only 0.146.
limits: Naive news retrieval, not a tuned pipeline. Differences between top models often not significant (pairwise bootstrapped p-values).
agent_relevance: Raw retrieval is not enough; later work shows search quality matters (see AIA).

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Two extrapolations to parity. Brier correlates with Chatbot Arena score and with log training compute.
limits: Few models, linear fit, wide intervals. The around-November-2026 date is a later FRI linear-trend update, not in this paper; I could not open that page.
agent_relevance: Gap is projected to close with scale, so the scaffold must add value beyond what the next base model brings.

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Crowd-of-LLMs ensemble: geometric mean of log odds was best aggregation.
numbers: Table 17 (appendix): median 0.197, trimmed mean 0.197, geometric mean 0.194, geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (2 SE about 0.024).
limits: Differences of 0.003 are inside the error bars.
agent_relevance: Aggregate samples in code with log-odds mean (G5).

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Superforecaster-written prompts were included as baselines (three prompts). They did not beat the plain scratchpad.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet with news: Superforecaster prompt 2 0.150; prompt 1 0.153; plain scratchpad 0.147 overall.
limits: Single model, N=6,389 forecasts; small differences.
agent_relevance: Human-expert prompt text is not a shortcut; match the process, not the persona.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Zero-shot frontier models are near no-skill on competition questions.
numbers: Test set Brier: random 0.250; best base model GPT-4-1106 0.208; human crowd 0.149.
quote: Most models scores are around or worse than random guessing (.25).
limits: Questions June 2023 to Jan 2024; crowd aggregate on same questions.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting gives little skill; track Brier against 0.25.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Full system (retrieval + fine-tuned reasoning + ensemble) closes most of the gap; ablations show what mattered.
numbers: Full system Brier 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (gap 0.03); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. No fine-tuning and no retrieval: 0.206 (back to baseline 0.208). One component ablated: 0.186.
limits: Hyperparameters tuned on validation; test is later in time. Backtested with a retrieval cutoff, which Paleka et al. show can leak.
agent_relevance: Closest published ancestor of an agent loop: retrieve, reason, sample many, aggregate in code.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: System beats the crowd where the crowd is unsure and loses where the crowd is sure.
numbers: Crowd forecast in .3 to .7: system .199 vs crowd .246. Under all three favorable conditions together (5+ articles, early retrieval dates, crowd uncertain): system .240 vs crowd .247. Crowd better when highly certain.
limits: Selective: conditions chosen post hoc; only a minority of forecasts qualify.
agent_relevance: Defer to a strong outside prior when it is extreme; spend reasoning effort on the uncertain middle.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Study 1: ensemble of 12 LLMs vs 925 human forecasters on 31 binary questions was statistically equivalent.
numbers: LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Exploratory equivalence test with d=0.5 bounds (0.081 Brier) passed (p=0.017 and 0.040).
quote: acquiescence effect, with mean model predictions being significantly above 50%
limits: Only 31 questions, low power; equivalence bound is wide (0.081 Brier is large). LLM mean predictions were above 50% (acquiescence) though outcomes were near even.
agent_relevance: Aggregation alone lifts weak individual models. Watch for a yes-bias and correct it.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Study 2: showing the human median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 improves them, but averaging beats letting the LLM update.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 to 0.14 (p=0.003); Claude 2 0.22 to 0.15 (p<0.001); gain 17 to 28%. Simple average of machine and human median beats the LLM update: GPT-4 0.13 (t(92)=2.583, p=.011), Claude 2 0.14 (t(92)=3.530, p=.001).
limits: Small question set.
agent_relevance: LLM updating on an outside forecast moves the right way but under-uses it; let code do the averaging (G5).

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering LLMs Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 1: 38 prompts over 4 models and 100 ForecastBench questions. Almost no prompt beats a minimal control after multiple-comparison correction.
numbers: Mixed-effects with Benjamini-Hochberg: Frequency-Based Reasoning (-0.014 Brier), Base Rate First (-0.011), Step-Back stayed better; Bayesian Reasoning (+0.030) and Propose-Evaluate-Select (+0.033) stayed worse (both p<0.001).
quote: encouraging the model to engage in Bayesian reasoning
limits: Effects about 0.01 Brier, tiny vs gaps of 0.017-0.05. Single 100-question set resolved end of 2024.
agent_relevance: Do not tell the agent to think Bayesian. A base-rate-first step is the only prompt-level gain, and it is small.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering LLMs Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 2: compound prompts and external prompts (including superforecaster-written, o1, o1-mini). Nothing helped after correction.
numbers: Brier: o1-mini 0.217, o1 0.216, Llama 3.1 405B 0.218, GPT-4o 0.208, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.207. Superforecaster-written Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt significantly worse (mean forecast 50%).
limits: Reasoning models (o1) were not better than GPT-4o here; 100 questions.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is a weak lever. Evidence, aggregation and calibration matter more.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Evaluation pitfalls: temporal leakage and extrapolation failures. Many LLM-matches-humans claims rest on flawed backtests.
numbers: At least 3.8% of Halawi et al. questions resolved early (no forecasting needed); at least 10% of Tao et al. (2025) trivial; auto-generated questions let a weak classifier reach over 80% on binary and 55% on 4-choice MCQ with a DeepSeek v3 pipeline.
quote: we should be careful about such conclusions
limits: Position paper; some judgments subjective.
agent_relevance: Treat backtest numbers as upper bounds. Only trust forward-resolved scores such as ForecastBench.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Brier scores are not comparable across datasets with different base rates; date-restricted search leaks.
numbers: Example: 50 questions at 50% base rate plus 50 at 5%: perfect on rare events gives total about 0.125; improving coin-flip questions 0.25 to 0.15 gives about 0.10 and looks better. Perplexity-based resolving has 1-5% error.
limits: Illustrative arithmetic; paper recommends reporting Brier, calibration and more.
agent_relevance: Log base rate with each forecast and compare against a base-rate forecaster, not only against 0.25.

source: Paleka et al. (2024/25) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Consistency (logical agreement across related questions) correlates with ground-truth Brier and can be measured instantly.
numbers: Arbitrage-based metric over 10 checks; some checks (conditional probabilities) correlate over R=0.9 with Brier; others little. 3,000-check benchmark resolving in 2028. Forecasters worse than 0.25 excluded.
limits: Few forecasters. ArbitrageForecaster improved optimized checks but not held-out checks and not Brier.
agent_relevance: Consistency checks are a cheap in-loop test (negation, conditional, paraphrase) but patching them does not make forecasts better.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions, frontier models match the crowd but trail Metaculus-hired experts.
numbers: o3 Brier 0.1352 vs human crowd 0.149 (Halawi) and 0.121 (Karger); experts (10 hired, 157 questions) mean Brier 0.1573, median 0.0225; held-out 41 questions mean 0.1222, median 0.0196. o3-pro 0.1307 on smaller set. Naive linear extrapolation reaches expert level before May 2027.
quote: far lower than o3 which got a score of 0.1352
limits: Paper compares expert MEDIAN Brier (0.0225) to model MEAN (0.1352); the expert MEAN 0.1573 is worse than o3. Experts answered 47% of questions. Author later replaced superforecaster with expert (trademark).
agent_relevance: Do not accept experts crush LLMs without checking mean vs median and question overlap.

source: Turtel et al. (2025, TMLR) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future
finding: Outcome-based RL (GRPO/ReMax) on prediction-market questions lets a 14B model match o1 and be better calibrated.
numbers: Soft-Brier: ReMax ensemble-7 0.190, Modified-GRPO 0.192, o1 0.202; ECE 0.062 / 0.054 / 0.093. Single run 0.199 (ECE 0.067). None beat Polymarket itself (market better by 0.039 to 0.051 Brier). Simulated Polymarket ROI over 10%.
limits: Questions with news headlines; trading edge depends on fees and bet rules; no model beat the market price alone.
agent_relevance: Calibration is trainable, but our agent does not train. Median of several samples at inference is the transferable part.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
finding: AIA Forecaster (agentic search + supervisor + Platt/extremization) reports parity with superforecasters on ForecastBench.
numbers: FB-7-21 Brier: AIA 0.1076, supers median 0.1110, public 0.1451, o3 0.133; FB-8-14: AIA 0.1099, supers 0.1152, ForecastBench SOTA 0.145; FB-Market: AIA 0.0753 vs supers 0.0740, market 0.0965. Hard liquid-market set: AIA 0.1258 vs market 0.1106 (worse), but ensemble with market beats market alone.
limits: Company technical report, not peer reviewed; point estimate lower than supers but CIs overlap; superforecaster baseline surveyed in 2024.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence that a scaffold, not a bigger model, can close the gap. Supports search, supervisor reconciliation, calibration.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster: Technical Report
finding: Component ablations: search quality, supervisor, ensembling, calibration.
numbers: Search none 0.1230; Search-A agentic 0.1140 (non-agentic 0.1174); Search-B agentic 0.1182. Single forecast 0.1182; mean 0.1140; median 0.1138. Supervisor agentic 0.1125 vs none 0.1199. Platt scaling 0.1076 vs none 0.1119. Market price + agentic search 0.075 vs price alone 0.096.
limits: Gains are 0.004-0.008 each; some tuned in-sample. Market price helps far more than news alone.
agent_relevance: Order of value: search > supervisor reconciliation > ensemble > Platt. Matches schema operators for evidence, reconcile, calibrate.

source: FutureSearch, Wildman et al. (2025) Bench to the Future: a pastcasting benchmark
finding: Bench to the Future: offline pastcasting with frozen web corpora avoids waiting for resolution; tracks model progress.
numbers: Metaculus questions, effective sample about 178.8 after down-weighting correlated ones. Claude Sonnet 3.5 0.1925 vs Sonnet 4 0.1560 (p=0.0024); Sonnet 3.7 0.1712; Sonnet 4 thinking 0.1597; Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1611. Sonnet 3.7 vs 4 not significant (p=0.139).
limits: Validity check on only 20 questions live vs retro; thinking mode did not clearly help (0.1645 vs 0.1712, p=0.17).
agent_relevance: Fast offline test bed for our scaffold without waiting months.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: ReAct agent with search and Python simulation matches the crowd; ensembling helps agents more than base models.
numbers: Brier: crowd 0.172 (acc 73.8%); RTF median of 3 0.169 (72.4%), mean of 3 0.170 (73.9%), single sampled 0.180; Halawi GPT-4o 0.177; base GPT-4o 0.210; base LM mean 0.218. Ensemble std 0.092 agent vs 0.150 base.
limits: Small test; own splits; preprint.
agent_relevance: Tool use (code for arithmetic and simulation) plus 3 samples is a cheap recipe with measured gain of about 0.04 Brier over base.

source: Yang et al. (2025) LLM-as-a-Prophet: Prophet Arena
finding: Prophet Arena: 1,367 resolved events, 72,136 markets; LLMs competitive far from resolution, markets win near it.
numbers: LLMs have small calibration errors; market baseline lags frontier LLMs at long horizons, then overtakes as resolution nears because markets absorb news faster. Raw Brier can mislead, need a baseline. Bottlenecks: wrong event recall, misread data sources.
limits: Per-model Brier not extracted; benchmark fixes the news given to models.
agent_relevance: Rely on the LLM for early reasoning; refresh evidence and re-forecast near deadline.

source: Chandak et al. (2026) Scaling Open-Ended Reasoning To Predict the Future (OpenForesight)
finding: Open-ended forecasting: 50,000 synthetic training questions from 250,000 news articles; RL on 8B model matches larger proprietary models.
numbers: OpenForecaster8B tested May-Aug 2025; offline CommonCrawl-news retrieval (cut one month before resolution) gives large gains; accuracy-only reward hurts calibration; Brier-only hurts exploration on hard questions.
limits: Exact accuracy numbers not extracted; model-graded answers.
agent_relevance: Track both accuracy and calibration; retrieval from a dated offline corpus is the leakage-safe design.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: Complex human forecasting strategies did NOT help LLMs; plain prompt beat the human market baseline on Brier only through a No bias.
numbers: Validation Brier: Human 0.1746, Basic 0.1955, Forecaster 0.2097, Breakdown 0.2053, Base Rates 0.2540, Both Sides 0.2159, Crowd 0.1860, News API 0.1950. Basic strong on No-resolved events (0.0503 vs human 0.0901), weak on Yes (0.3407 vs 0.2592).
quote: models tendency to guess that most events are unlikely to occur
limits: Single dataset; most events resolve No so low-guess bias looks good.
agent_relevance: Report Brier separately for Yes and No resolved cases (weighted Brier) to catch a low-guess habit.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Autocast (2022): early baseline showing the gap; retrieval + fine-tuned T5 beat 2022 baselines but not humans.
numbers: Best ML binary accuracy 65% vs 92% human crowd (random 50%); calibration error largest FiD Static 40% vs human crowd 8%, cut to 17% when fed crowd predictions (FiD Temporal). UnifiedQA zero-shot near random.
limits: Pre-GPT-4 models; accuracy metric, not Brier.
agent_relevance: Crowd predictions as input help calibration, a pattern repeated by FRI freeze values.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) FutureX: live benchmark for LLM agents in future prediction
finding: FutureX: live benchmark for LLM agents, daily updates, 25 models including Deep Research agents; four difficulty levels.
numbers: Levels 1-4 from basic single-choice to open-ended high-volatility Super Agent events; scores July 20 to Aug 3 2025. Failure modes: fake web pages and temporal validity. Per-model figures not extracted.
limits: Abstract and design read; numeric leaderboard not extracted; scoring is accuracy/F1-like, not Brier.
agent_relevance: Live agent runs expose web-trust failures; add source-reliability checks in the evidence step.

source: ForecastBench website (forecastbench.org) leaderboard pages
finding: Leaderboard structure: tournament board (tools allowed, crowd value for market questions) and baseline board (no tools). Parity projection uses a linear trend.
numbers: Metric: difficulty-adjusted Brier turned into Brier Index 0-100%; rank = equal-weight mean of dataset and market scores. Humans last surveyed July 2024; models added 50 days after submission.
limits: Landing pages had no tables, so the 0.017 gap and November 2026 parity date could not be verified.
agent_relevance: Cite the 0.017 gap and Nov 2026 date only as FRI claims; check the live explore page first.

source: Karger et al. (2025, ICLR) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities
finding: Claimed later FRI update: gap to superforecasters 0.017 Brier, about one year of LLM progress, parity around Nov 2026. Taken from the subfield brief; not opened.
numbers: 0.017 Brier gap; wide interval
limits: Not read; web search quota exhausted and forecastbench.org pages returned no tables.
agent_relevance: Planning guess only: the scaffold should be valuable even after base-model parity.
